The novel behind the questions.

SOMED.AI is a philosophical techno-thriller by Gabriel Mejia Mory. Aden and Irene are drawn into a secret effort pushing intelligence toward a historic threshold, and others are racing to reach it first.

Everything on this account, our POSSIBLE FUTURES series, is an original thought experiment inspired by the book's questions: who benefits when the future can be predicted, and who pays.

He already knows how this ends. She doesn't.

POSSIBLE FUTURES 01 / LOVE. In this possible future, an app can forecast whether a relationship will last. He checked. She was never asked.

Would you check? And if you did, would you tell them?

An original thought experiment, not a scene from the book. It's inspired by SOMED.AI, a philosophical techno-thriller by Gabriel Mejia Mory about a secret project to build a system that can model the future, and the fight over who benefits from what it knows.

Certainty or discovery?

A forecast could spare you years with the wrong person. It could also turn the person you love into a score they never agreed to.

Swipe for the case for it, the cost, and who pays. Save it for the next time someone says they'd "just want to know."

The last time she packed these boxes, she was leaving.

THE OTHER SIDE / 01 LOVE. Yesterday we asked whether you'd check a forecast of your relationship. Today, the strongest case for yes: not checking in secret, but checking together, after you've already been blindsided once.

If you both agreed, would you look?

With 300 of your likes, a computer judged your personality better than your own spouse.

That's real. A 2015 study of 86,220 people found 10 likes beat a coworker's judgment, 70 a friend's, 150 a family member's (per PNAS, Stanford & Cambridge).

Somed.ai asks what happens when it goes further.

In 2013, scientists planted a false memory in a living brain.

That's real. MIT researchers used light to reactivate the brain cells holding a mouse's memory of a safe room while it got a mild shock elsewhere. Afterwards, the mouse feared the safe room, where nothing had ever happened to it (per Science / MIT News).

Somed.ai asks what happens when it goes further: "It would edit me."

About 1 in 4 people came to 'remember' a childhood event that never happened.

That's real. In Elizabeth Loftus's original 'lost in the mall' study, a false story mixed with true family memories was enough for about a quarter of adults to recall it. Later research debates how strong those memories were (per Wellcome Collection, Neuroscience News).
